body_markdown:
A mosquito-borne disease that is commonly associated with tropical and subtropical regions is attracting attention in Florida after health officials reported locally acquired cases. Dengue fever, sometimes called “breakbone fever” because of the intense muscle, joint and bone pain it can cause, is becoming an increasingly important public health concern in parts of the United States.


What makes the recent situation notable is not simply the number of dengue infections being reported. It is the fact that some people appear to have contracted the virus locally rather than while traveling abroad.


## Dengue Is No Longer Only a Travel-Related Concern


Dengue is caused by a virus transmitted through the bites of infected mosquitoes. Historically, many dengue cases identified in the United States have involved people who recently traveled to regions where the disease is more widespread, including parts of the Caribbean, Central and South America, Southeast Asia and the Pacific Islands.


However, locally acquired infections are also being documented.


According to the supplied report, 893 dengue cases have been reported across the United States this year. Of those cases, 40 were acquired locally within the country. Florida accounted for 39 of those locally acquired infections, while another case was reported in Virginia. The Florida cases were identified in several counties along the state's west coast, including Citrus, Pinellas and Hillsborough counties.


The development does not necessarily mean that dengue is spreading widely throughout Florida or the United States. Instead, it highlights the possibility that infected mosquitoes can transmit the virus in areas where the appropriate mosquito species are present.


## Why Dengue Can Be So Unpleasant


Many people infected with dengue may not develop noticeable symptoms. For those who do become sick, however, the illness can be extremely uncomfortable.


Reported symptoms can include a high fever, headaches, nausea, skin rashes and severe aches throughout the body. The nickname “breakbone fever” comes from the sometimes extreme pain experienced in the muscles, joints and bones.


In most cases, people recover with supportive care. Nevertheless, dengue can occasionally progress into a severe and potentially life-threatening illness.


The supplied source states that approximately one in 20 people with dengue develops severe symptoms. These complications can include serious bleeding, a dangerous fall in blood pressure and organ failure. Severe illness can develop rapidly, which is why people with concerning symptoms should seek medical attention rather than attempting to manage a potentially serious infection on their own.


## The Mosquitoes Behind Dengue Transmission


Dengue is primarily spread by Aedes mosquitoes. These mosquitoes are also capable of transmitting other diseases, including Zika and yellow fever.


Aedes mosquitoes are established across significant parts of the southeastern and southwestern United States. The source report also points to rising temperatures as one factor that may increase the areas suitable for these mosquitoes.


One statistic highlighted in the report is particularly striking. Researchers have estimated that roughly 75% of the United States could provide suitable conditions for these mosquito species.


That does not mean three-quarters of the country is experiencing dengue transmission. Instead, it indicates that the environmental conditions needed by the mosquitoes may exist across a much larger area than many people might assume.


The United States experienced a particularly large increase in dengue cases in 2024, when reported infections rose substantially above the average recorded over the previous two decades. Local infections have also been documented in states including Florida, California and Texas, while New Jersey experienced a dengue outbreak in 2024.


## What People Can Do to Reduce Their Risk


Because dengue is transmitted by mosquitoes, preventing mosquito bites remains one of the most important ways to reduce the risk of infection.


People living in areas where Aedes mosquitoes are present can take several practical precautions. Using insect repellent can help reduce bites, while wearing loose-fitting clothing that covers the arms and legs provides an additional physical barrier.


It is also important to consider the environment around the home.


Standing water can provide mosquitoes with places to breed. Containers, buckets, plant pots and other objects that collect rainwater should therefore be checked and emptied regularly. Holes or objects around a property that can hold water can also contribute to mosquito breeding.


These measures may seem simple, but reducing mosquito populations around homes can form an important part of community-level disease prevention.


## What Travelers Should Know


Dengue remains a significant concern for people traveling to regions where the virus is commonly circulating.


Travelers should take precautions against mosquito bites during their trip. Recommended measures include using insect repellent, wearing appropriate clothing and, where necessary, sleeping under mosquito nets.


An important consideration is that someone who becomes infected while traveling can potentially contribute to local transmission after returning home if they are bitten by mosquitoes capable of carrying dengue.


This makes mosquito-bite prevention important not only during travel but also after returning from a dengue-risk area.


## Is There a Dengue Treatment?


There is no specific cure for dengue described in the supplied source. Treatment generally focuses on managing symptoms and preventing complications.


Rest and adequate hydration are important, while acetaminophen may be used to help manage fever and pain. People who develop severe illness may require hospital treatment and intravenous fluids.


Anyone who develops symptoms that could be consistent with dengue, particularly after travel to an affected region or possible exposure to infected mosquitoes, should speak with a healthcare professional. Severe symptoms require prompt medical attention.


## Why Florida's Cases Matter


The locally acquired cases in Florida are a reminder that mosquito-borne diseases can appear in places where people may not traditionally expect them.


The presence of dengue in Florida does not mean residents should panic. It does, however, reinforce the importance of mosquito control, disease surveillance and awareness of symptoms.


Public health authorities have emphasized the need for continued monitoring and preparedness in areas where mosquitoes capable of transmitting dengue are established.


For individuals, the most practical response is straightforward: reduce mosquito exposure, eliminate standing water around the home and take appropriate precautions when traveling.


As mosquito populations and environmental conditions change, diseases historically associated with tropical regions may receive greater attention in other parts of the world. Florida's recent locally acquired dengue cases demonstrate why monitoring these infections remains important.
